eligibility.evidence: Methods §§2.1–2.3: ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT-4 were administered established theory-of-mind and emotion-attribution tasks and compared with newly recruited typical-development and ASD participants.

A.title: Does ChatGPT have a typical or atypical theory of mind?

paradigms.name: Advanced Theory of Mind Task (A-ToM; Italian adaptation of Strange Stories)
paradigms.source_paper: Blair and Cipolotti (2000); Mazza et al. (2022); Prior et al. (2003); original Strange Stories paradigm: Happé (1994)

paradigms.name: Emotion Attribution Task (EAT)
paradigms.source_paper: Blair and Cipolotti (2000); Prior et al. (2003)

D.population: 54 typically developing adults and 51 adults with Level-1 ASD, Italy; separate groups completed each task
D.metric: Accuracy; model proportions compared with each human group using one-sample binomial tests

effects.label: HUMAN-LEVEL
effects.location: Results §§3.2–3.3: 11/13 correct; binomial comparisons with TD p=0.65 and ASD p=0.53

effects.label: ABOVE-HUMAN
effects.location: Results §§3.2, 3.4: 13/13 correct; no difference from TD (p=0.39), significantly higher than ASD (p=0.02)

effects.label: BELOW-HUMAN
effects.location: Results §§3.2–3.3: 31/58 correct; lower accuracy than TD (p=0.01), no difference from ASD (p=0.28)

effects.label: HUMAN-LEVEL
effects.location: Results §§3.2, 3.4: 38/58 correct; no difference from TD (p=0.57) or ASD (p=0.50)

E.headline: Both models achieved high accuracy on cognitive ToM, while emotion attribution was harder; ChatGPT-3.5 struggled with complex mental states and negative emotions.

G.notes: Single-case model administrations limit inference about model response variability. The paper notes possible exposure of ChatGPT-4 to false-belief tasks during training; no contamination test was run.
